models.collectorNote: Early cars are the value play; Nismo and the final Premium T-spec cars are where collectors are already looking. Check launch-control history and transmission service records before anything else.

generations.name: Early R35
generations.note: The shock launch car. Under $70k in the US at debut, quicker than a Porsche 911 Turbo in most tests, and heavy in a way it somehow turned into grip.

generations.name: Facelift R35
generations.note: The 2017 refresh softened the cabin and sharpened the face, and output rose to 565 hp. The Nismo made 600 hp and cost supercar money, because by then, that was the competition.

models.intro: Nissan's giant-killer, built for 17 years with one brief: be faster than cars costing three times as much. It mostly was. All-wheel drive, a hand-built twin-turbo V6, and a launch-control party trick that never got old.

models.collectorNote: Clean S30s and twin-turbo Z32s are properly collectible now. The current Z is the sensible new buy, same engine, warranty, no 30-year-old rubber.

generations.name: 240Z
generations.note: The car that proved Japan could build a sports car the world wanted. Styled like a European GT, priced like an American one, and reliable in a way neither managed.

generations.name: 300ZX
generations.note: Twin turbos, four-wheel steering on Turbo models, and a design so clean it shares its headlights with a Lamborghini Diablo. Still looks modern. It isn't, budget accordingly.

generations.name: Nissan Z
generations.note: Nissan dropped the number and kept the recipe: twin-turbo V6, rear drive, and a standard manual. Old-school on purpose, and better for it.

models.intro: The people's sports car, running since 1969 with a long nap in the middle. The 240Z made performance democratic; the current car keeps the twin-turbo, rear-drive, manual-gearbox faith alive when most rivals dropped it.
models.name: Z

models.collectorNote: The US 25-year import rule made R32s common and R34s legal in stages through the 2020s. Verify import paperwork and Japanese auction history carefully, R34 prices leave no room for surprises.

generations.name: R32 GT-R
generations.note: Group A rules built this car, and it won everything, 29 straight wins in Japanese touring cars. All-wheel drive, twin turbos, and the 'Godzilla' nickname, earned in Australia.

generations.name: R33 GT-R
generations.note: The bigger, stiffer, less loved middle child, which makes it the value pick of the three. It was also the first production car to lap the Nürburgring in under eight minutes.

generations.name: R34 GT-R
generations.note: The poster car. A dashboard display showing g-forces and boost in 1999 felt like science fiction, and the V-spec cars are now some of the most expensive Japanese cars ever sold.

models.intro: Three generations of Skyline GT-R that never officially came to America, which only sharpened the legend. The RB26 engine's official 276 hp was a gentlemen's-agreement fiction everyone politely maintained.
models.name: Skyline GT-R

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The first mass-market modern EV, launched before most rivals had a programme. Early 24 kWh cars are now very cheap, because the range is what it is. Check the battery health bars, not the odometer.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: More range, more power, and the longer-range Plus model. Still air-cooled battery chemistry, which is why hot-climate cars age faster. Priced as transport, not as a tech product.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Reborn as a raised crossover with proper range and a liquid-cooled battery. Whether it can repeat the original's first-mover trick in a crowded field is the open question.

models.intro: The car that proved ordinary people would buy an electric car if it was priced like a car. First-generation cars depreciate like dropped phones, which makes a healthy-battery example one of the cheapest ways to run a second car there is.
models.name: Leaf

generations.name: GU Patrol
generations.note: The overlander's Patrol: live axles, a ladder frame, and the 4.8L petrol six beloved in the Middle East. Still in production for some markets decades after launch.

generations.name: Y62
generations.note: Independent suspension and a 5.6L V8 moved the Patrol upmarket without losing the plot. Sold in the US as the Nissan Armada, same truck, different badge.

generations.name: Current Patrol
generations.note: The V8 is gone, replaced by a twin-turbo V6 with more power and a nine-speed automatic. The formula, big frame, big cabin, desert-proof cooling, is unchanged.

models.intro: Land Cruiser's oldest rival, and in much of the Middle East and Australia, the preferred one. The Patrol is what UN fleets and desert drivers buy when a breakdown is not a survivable option.
models.name: Patrol
